d

decision.explanation: Set u=x+1 and v=y-1, so x=u-1 and y=v+1. Substitution gives u'=(u-1)^2+3(u-1)+(v+1)+1=u^2+u+v and v'=-3(u-1)-(v+1)^2+2(v+1)-4=-3u-v^2. Thus option c shifts the equilibrium to the origin.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+3x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+2y(t)-4\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[-1,\,1]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
after.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)-1,\,y(t)=v(t)+1,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)+3x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)-1)^{2}+3(u(t)-1)+(v(t)+1)+1 \\  & =({u}^{2}(t)-2u(t)+1)+3u(t)-3+v(t)+1+1 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-3x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+2y(t)-4 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =-3(u(t)-1)-(v(t)+1)^{2}+2(v(t)+1)-4 \\  & =-3u(t)+3-({v}^{2}(t)+2v(t)+1)+2v(t)+2-4 \\  & =-3u(t)-{v}^{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=-3u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)-1,\,y(t)=v(t)+1,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)+3x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)-1)^{2}+3(u(t)-1)+(v(t)+1)+1 \\  & =({u}^{2}(t)-2u(t)+1)+3u(t)-3+v(t)+1+1 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-3x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+2y(t)-4 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =-3(u(t)-1)-(v(t)+1)^{2}+2(v(t)+1)-4 \\  & =-3u(t)+3-({v}^{2}(t)+2v(t)+1)+2v(t)+2-4 \\  & =-3u(t)-{v}^{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=-3u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[1,\,2]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
after.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)+1,\,y(t)=v(t)+2,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)+{y}^{2}(t)-3x(t)-y(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)+1)^{2}+(v(t)+2)^{2}-3(u(t)+1)-(v(t)+2) \\  & =({u}^{2}(t)+2u(t)+1)+({v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+4)-3u(t)-3-v(t)-2 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)-u(t)+{v}^{2}(t)+3v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =2x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+5y(t)-8 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =2(u(t)+1)-(v(t)+2)^{2}+5(v(t)+2)-8 \\  & =2u(t)+2-({v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+4)+5v(t)+10-8 \\  & =2u(t)+v(t)-{v}^{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)-u(t)+{v}^{2}(t)+3v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=2u(t)+v(t)-{v}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[1,\,2]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
content.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)+1,\,y(t)=v(t)+2,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)+{y}^{2}(t)-3x(t)-y(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)+1)^{2}+(v(t)+2)^{2}-3(u(t)+1)-(v(t)+2) \\  & =({u}^{2}(t)+2u(t)+1)+({v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+4)-3u(t)-3-v(t)-2 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)-u(t)+{v}^{2}(t)+3v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =2x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+5y(t)-8 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =2(u(t)+1)-(v(t)+2)^{2}+5(v(t)+2)-8 \\  & =2u(t)+2-({v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+4)+5v(t)+10-8 \\  & =2u(t)+v(t)-{v}^{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)-u(t)+{v}^{2}(t)+3v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=2u(t)+v(t)-{v}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
After shifting a linear system, the eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors remain unchanged.

Thus, the matrix $B$ in the shifted system has the same eigenvectors as the system's matrix in the original coordinates. These eigenvectors are ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2},$ or any nonzero vectors that are parallel to them.

before.html:
Question 4
?

A linear system of ODEs has an equilibrium at x∗. One of the nullclines of the system has the equation y=−4x+1 in the corresponding phase space. The system is then shifted using u=x−x∗. Which of the following is guaranteed to be a nullcline of the shifted system?

a
y=−4x+1
b
y=−x
c
y=4x
d
y=−4x
e
y=x−4
Submit

decision.explanation: The equilibrium (x*,y*) lies on the nullcline, so y*=-4x*+1. With u=x-x* and v=y-y*, substitution gives v+y*=-4(u+x*)+1, hence v=-4u. In the displayed coordinate notation, this is y=-4x, option d.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A linear system of ODEs has an equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}.$ One of the nullclines of the system has the equation $y=-4x+1$ in the corresponding phase space. The system is then shifted using $u=x-{x}^{∗}.$ Which of the following is **guaranteed** to be a nullcline of the shifted system?
after.worked_solution:
After shifting a system, the geometric structure of the vector field is preserved. In particular, each nullcline is translated but retains its orientation, meaning its slope does not change.

Because the equilibrium is moved to the origin by the shift, the translated nullclines must pass through the origin in the shifted coordinates.

Thus, the nullclines of the shifted system pass through the origin and have the same slopes as the corresponding nullclines of the original system.

Among the given options, the only line that satisfies the above conditions is $y=-4x.$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: A system of ODEs has an unstable saddle point at ${x}^{∗}.$ The system is then shifted using $u=x-{x}^{∗}.$ Which of the following best describes the point $(0,0)$ for the shifted system?
after.worked_solution:
Shifting does not alter the local behavior near an equilibrium. So, the equilibrium retains its original classification (saddle, node, spiral, center, etc.).

Recall that the shift moves the equilibrium to the origin.

Thus, the equilibrium at $(0,0)$ in the shifted system has the same classification as ${x}^{∗}$ in the original system.

Therefore, the correct answer is "An unstable saddle point".
